references.text: The direct follow-up where Jacob's household hands over the foreign gods and the earrings, which Jacob buries under the terebinth at Shechem.
Joshua urges the people to remove the gods their fathers served and to serve the Lord – a clear parallel to Jacob's instruction to his family.
Joshua commands the people to remove the foreign gods among them and turn their hearts to the Lord, almost identical to Jacob's appeal.
Samuel commands Israel to remove foreign gods and Asherah images from their midst and turn their hearts to the Lord – a clear parallel to Jacob's words.
The Lord commands Moses to consecrate the people and have them wash their clothes – paralleling Jacob's call for cleansing and changing garments.
The believers in Ephesus burn their books related to occultism, an act that reflects the biblical principle of removing idolatry from their midst.
Both texts connect sanctification with the removal of impurities in order to meet God.
Repetition of the motif: Separating oneself from what is foreign or unclean as a prerequisite for belonging to God.
Both texts define true repentance as an active rejection and removal of idols.
Theological continuity in the requirement to separate from impurities in order to receive God.
Identical command to cast away idols as a prerequisite for serving God.
